story_text.value:
Algeon is a query engine built on Apache DataFusion that exposes NVIDIA's cuGraph, cuVS, and cuML as SQL table functions. It doesn't write its GPU kernels. Instead, it takes what NVIDIA already has and embeds it into DataFusion, so you can call those GPU operations on any arbitrary data, with filter/join/agg using plain SQL.

And why would you want that? Because GPU analytics used to require ad-hoc ETL pipelines, Python glue code, and imperative operation calls. That makes it hard to fit into a backend API service, and it isn't flexible enough for frequent exploratory iteration, adapting to different search conditions and data. Think of agents trying to answer complex questions on a datalake, which involves not only relational operations, but also graph/vector/ML analytics. They can now use declarative SQL to test their hypotheses and build the next query based on the previous response, making GPU OLAP an interactive service. Algeon can also be used as a library living inside your backend service, so your query response can be used directly within a single process, saving the transfer cost between the query engine and backend service.

I started building Algeon last year. At first, it was cuDF Rust FFI bindings that aimed to bring GPU ETL pipelines into a single backend process, and it worked very well. Then I realized it might be possible to move GPU data science workloads into an OLAP query engine, since the NVIDIA RAPIDS ecosystem and DataFusion are mature.

For use cases, architecture design, benchmarks, and more, feel free to check out, any feedback is welcome https://algeon.dev/

story_text.value:
I’ve spent the last year building context for AI analysts in the mid-market. I’ve open sourced a library from my learnings, along the same principles of the Matt Pocock skills.

Principles:

* Claude / Codex / Cursor etc are great data agents - you just need context to enable them to answer business questions correctly.

* Much of the important context lives in analysts heads'

* Context must be maintainable (short, human readable - markdown and yaml)

* Added context should be load bearing, not repeat of information that is available in another source of truth - and evaluations prove the value of the context

* Companies should own their own context, and must be shareable with any model

* Context should be version controlled (and github works as a context store).

What the library does:

* Performs an interview with your analysts (context-interview skill), one domain at a time, similar to what I have done as a consultant. The interview is informed by your query logs.

* The AI develops evaluation questions at the same time as building the context - and at the end of each domain interview asks you to run an evaluation with and without the context. The evaluation will actually check the results against your dashboards if you allow it. We have shown increases in accuracy from 87% to 95% by adding this context in our imaginary open-source company, Shorelane.

* Provides a set of skills to use the context that follow best practices for self service analytics:

  * Write a plain english plan for the business user to approve

  * Execute the plan

  * Verify that the execution followed the plan, and provide a simple uncertainty score. 

  * Enable a adversarial review of the answer if their are doubts.
What you get:

Context repo written in markdown and yaml after you finish the interview. We use a single github repo, divided into domains. The interview can be shared and restarted by checking in/out of github.

A set of skills to share with your business team

Optional: We offer a fast MCP server to serve the Github-based context to your team.

story_text.value:
This is a project I've been working on for about 8 months now. I worked in legal tech for 3 years and found that one of the biggest hurdles for AI agents and lawyers alike when doing legal research is tracking changes, and correctly cross referencing those changes between different forms of legal documents.

W2D builds a SQLite dataset from public sources, and offers agent skills for answering questions about that dataset.

The dataset holds multiple revisions of the U.S. Code at each release point that you add. It holds the public laws that amend the Code, and it links each amendment to the change that it made. It holds court opinions from CourtListener, by page and paragraph, and it links each U.S.C. citation to the provision that the court cited. It can also hold House roll calls.

This is similar in spirit to "git for Law" but includes a lot more utilities than diffs to make it an effective tool for research.

title.value: Show HN: Local, Tracked, Versioned, Legal Research Databases

story_text.value:
I was wondering how those classic demoscene effects come out in different languages. It’s interesting to see the required contortions for each language to get there. For example, SQLite has no float32, so it's emulated in SQL. Wasm has no sin(), so the hand-written port builds its own sine table, to name a few.
It was built end-to-end by AI agents. Every port is checked pixel by pixel against the C reference by a script in the repo.

hi everyone, as an avid public transportation enjoyer and mini motorways fan ive always had an itch to make a metro optimization game, so i made this daily puzzle

fun part for me: after a grad pl course i wasnt sure when id ever use a sat solver. turns out here. every daily map is solved exactly with or-tools cp-sat before it ships so theres always a proven best score to chase (hidden unless you turn on hints)

maps get tougher through the week. mon/tue easy, wed/thu medium, fri hard, sat/sun bigger bonus maps with extra features. you can replay old maps via play archives. no account no ads

ive only tested with friends and family who arent big puzzle players so id love feedback. im leaving out instructions on purpose to see how well the game teaches itself

let me know any and all thoughts!

story_text.value:
I built a small browser incremental game where you start by answering tasks at your desk to save up to rent a GPU, and hire a real Qwen3-0.6B model running locally in your browser over WebGPU (~358 MB download).

Throughout the game you buy upgrades to your model's harness, things like JSON structured output or date tools. This actually changes how the model behaves. You can even write your own prompts.

It uses MLC WebLLM on Chrome and a custom WebGPU inference engine and BPE tokenizer on Firefox (because shader buffer limitations)

I also did a write-up here: https://simedw.com/2026/10/27/harness-corp/

story_text.value:
Since AI has grown in popularity, technical and non-technical employees have been using it to build small tools and apps to boost productivity and model prototypes. Some companies like Ramp and Stripe, are building their own internal platform for this. That’s great for them, but not every company can, or has the bandwidth to do that.

Pando is a similar idea, but fully open-source. It provides a home for these apps and tools that people build, so they get put in a centralized place with a clear owner. Apps are automatically put behind company SSO, scanned for vulnerabilities, isolated, and easily shareable. You can also put egress controls on them, and control how many apps people can deploy.

Since it’s API first, there is a native CLI and MCP for it, that makes deploying super easy.

Curious if this is something you are running into at your company, and if Pando sounds interesting to you! And if it doesn’t, why not?

story_text.value:
For the past two decades I've been looking for something that allows me to easily build complex and pretty UIs in places that are generally hostile to complex and pretty UIs aka game engines. Solutions do exists but they either include awkward pricing structures or required embedding something like CEF. Though it would be interesting to see how far QuickJS, Yoga and Skia take me so decided to conjure something up with the help of Claude.

While the system is geared towards games there is nothing preventing one from using it to build standalone apps.

Perf wise the system is starting to be pretty good and on native most of the time beats chrome rendering the same UI. When embedded inside games it usually adds about +0.04 / +0.08 ms per frame. WASM/WebGPU still has lots of optimisation especially when it comes to the pipeline compilations (lag when you first start using the site).

Additional bonus is that LLM get trained with massive amounts of HTML and React code that readily available while engine specific UI code mostly benefits from general UI patterns LLMs have learned elsewhere.

More practical demos: - https://orktes.github.io/jsui/three/ - https://orktes.github.io/jsui/demo/

I've had the dream of building this for a while and it definitely would not have been possible without Opus 5.5.

story_text.value:
Security should be free! I was getting mad that all the security tools that meant to guard your agents are not local and those who are, just cost a fortune.

So I’ve built Weir. You can watch you sensitive data flow, your traces and your egress tools calls.

It doesn’t stop your ADLC, it only watch it locally (no egress).

The agents you use - I’ve set a Claude code hook that stripe your known keys from tool output before the model sees them.

The agents you build - Weir plants fake keys, runs your agents flows and report every place they leaked (traces, logs, model, services). It helped me find CVE-2026-116691 in MLFlow.

Would be super happy to know what you guys think!

title.value: Show HN: Keep your credentials out of the AI agents you use and build
